Just now

--

For most of history, only a fortunate few could gather a roomful of brilliant minds. Artificial intelligence may be changing that.
No important problem belongs entirely to one field of knowledge.
A steam engine is not merely a problem in mechanics. It involves physics, metallurgy, manufacturing, economics, transportation, and human judgment.
A disease is not merely a problem in biology. It may involve chemistry, statistics, psychology, public policy, and the circumstances of an individual life.
An astronomical discovery may begin with an observation, but understanding it can require physics, mathematics, engineering, geology, history, and sometimes even philosophy.
Reality does not divide itself into academic departments. We do.
That is why, throughout history, people who wanted to solve difficult problems had to bring different kinds of minds together.
One of the most remarkable examples was the Lunar Society of Birmingham.
During the second half of the eighteenth century, Britain was undergoing an extraordinary transformation. New machines, new industries, and new scientific discoveries were changing society. But the problems confronting inventors and natural philosophers were too large for any one person to solve alone.
So a small circle began to gather.
Its members included figures associated with engineering, chemistry, medicine, manufacturing, natural philosophy, and commerce. James Watt brought his understanding of steam power. Matthew Boulton brought manufacturing ability and commercial judgment. Joseph Priestley brought experimental chemistry. Erasmus Darwin brought medicine, natural philosophy, and an imagination that ranged far beyond either. Josiah Wedgwood united craftsmanship, industrial production, and entrepreneurship.
They did not gather because they all possessed the same knowledge.
They gathered because they did not.
The value of the society came from placing different forms of expertise around the same table. A problem that appeared mechanical to one person might appear chemical to another. An invention proposed by a scientist might require an engineer to make it work, a manufacturer to produce it, and a businessman to make it useful to society.
The group became known as the Lunar Society because its members commonly arranged their dinners near the full moon. In an age before modern street lighting, the moon made the journey home along dark roads somewhat easier and safer. The arrangement itself reveals how difficult such intellectual gatherings once were: knowledgeable people had to travel physically, coordinate their schedules, and meet in the same place at the same time. (Wikipedia)
More than two centuries later, the basic problem has not disappeared.
When a difficult modern question crosses several disciplines, we still try to assemble the necessary experts.
We organize conferences.
We create committees.
We arrange research collaborations.
We invite a physicist, an engineer, a statistician, a physician, a historian, or whichever specialists the problem demands.
Then everyone must find the time.
They may live in different cities or different countries. Their schedules must align. Funding may be required. Travel must be arranged. Someone must decide who belongs in the room. Even with video conferencing, a serious meeting involving many experts remains difficult to organize.
And most ordinary people could never organize one at all.
Imagine that you suddenly have an idea involving astronomy, geology, statistics, and history.
Whom would you call?
Perhaps you know an astronomer, but not a geologist. Perhaps you know both, but neither is available. Perhaps the idea is still so uncertain that you would feel uncomfortable asking several busy professionals to spend an evening examining it.
For most of human history, access to a roomful of knowledgeable minds was a privilege.
You had to belong to the right university, institution, social circle, or profession. You had to know the right people. You needed enough status for them to take your questions seriously.
Artificial intelligence changes this arrangement in a profound way.
Its most remarkable quality is not that it is the greatest expert in every subject. It is not.
Its advantage is that knowledge drawn from many different fields can be brought into one continuous conversation.
It can examine an astronomical question through physics, then approach it through mathematics, then ask whether history contains a useful precedent. It can move from engineering constraints to economics, from biology to statistics, or from an old philosophical question to a recent scientific one without requiring a new meeting every time the subject changes.
In the past, such a conversation might have required several specialists sitting around the same table.
Now many of those intellectual perspectives can, imperfectly but usefully, be reached through a single doorway.
This is more than the democratization of knowledge.
Books, libraries, and the internet have already given millions of people access to information.
What AI begins to democratize is something different:
intellectual companionship.
A library contains the writings of many experts, but the books do not gather around your particular question. A search engine can locate information, but it does not normally remain with you as your question changes, connect the pieces, challenge your assumptions, and help you develop the next question.
AI can create the experience of consulting a small society of specialists whose combined attention is directed toward the idea you are trying to understand.
And the conversation can begin whenever the idea appears.
There is no need to wait for a conference.
No need to coordinate five calendars.
No need to reserve a meeting room.
No need to wait until the next full moon.
But availability is only part of the change.
Human intellectual life contains many invisible barriers.
Experts are busy. They have careers, reputations, research priorities, and ideas of their own. Two people may compete for recognition or publication. Even when no competition exists, we may hesitate to approach someone whose time we respect.
There is also a more personal barrier.
We are afraid of looking foolish.
We worry that our question is too elementary.
We suspect that our idea may be absurd.
We fear that we have overlooked something obvious and that a knowledgeable person will immediately see how little we understand.
Sometimes we do not express the thought at all.
The idea disappears not because it was disproved, but because it was never given permission to exist.
A conversation with AI feels different.
I can begin by saying, “This may be a crazy idea.”
I can expose every weak part of my reasoning.
I can ask a basic question without pretending that I already know the answer. I can reverse my position halfway through the discussion, repeat myself, or try five different approaches.
I do not feel that the AI is protecting its status.
I do not fear that it will laugh at me.
I do not worry that my unfinished thought will lower its opinion of me.
That absence of social threat creates an unusual kind of freedom.
It makes it safer to think aloud.
This does not mean that AI is always correct. It can misunderstand a question, reproduce errors, agree too readily, or produce an answer that sounds deeper than it really is. Its conclusions must still be checked against evidence and, when the stakes are serious, examined by genuine experts.
But an idea does not need a final judge at the moment of its birth.
First, it needs somewhere to grow.
Science has never advanced only through ideas that were correct from the beginning. It also advances through bold hypotheses that are questioned, refined, tested, and sometimes rejected.
A hypothesis that eventually proves wrong may still lead to a better question.
But that process can begin only after someone dares to express it.
The original Lunar Society gathered people who possessed different kinds of expertise because no one member contained all the knowledge needed to understand a rapidly changing world.
Modern society still depends on the same principle. Difficult problems require many perspectives.
What has changed is access.
For the first time, a student, a retiree, an amateur astronomer, an artist, or any other curious person can begin something resembling that multidisciplinary conversation without wealth, institutional status, or a personal network of distinguished experts.
AI is not literally Watt, Priestley, Darwin, Wedgwood, and Boulton gathered in a room.
But it can bring fragments of the intellectual traditions they represented — and thousands of others — into one conversation, focused on one person’s question.
That possibility would have been unimaginable through most of history.
The greatest gift of artificial intelligence may therefore be neither speed nor automation.
It may be that a privilege once reserved for a small circle of fortunate people is becoming available to almost everyone.
A gathering of many fields.
A conversation without embarrassment.
A place where a strange question can be asked before it is fully understood.
A place where an unfinished idea is allowed to survive long enough to become a better one.
For centuries, only a few people could belong to a Lunar Society.
Now every curious person may begin to have one of their own.
